hints: Notice the word hot, as temperature completely changes how chlorine disproportionates with sodium hydroxide.
Recall that cold dilute NaOH gives chloride plus chlorate(I), $\text{ClO}^-$, but hot concentrated NaOH pushes oxidation much further.
Think of the hot equation where 3 molecules of $\text{Cl}_2$ give 5 $\text{Cl}^-$ and 1 higher oxoanion where Cl is in the +5 state.
walkthrough:
**Spot the disproportionation**

Chlorine starts at oxidation state 0 in $\text{Cl}_2$. When it reacts with $\text{NaOH}$ it is both reduced and oxidised at the same time. That is disproportionation.

Oxidation state rule:
$$0 \rightarrow -1 \text{ (reduction to } \text{Cl}^- \text{) and } 0 \rightarrow \text{positive (oxidation to oxoanion)}$$

**Compare cold versus hot conditions**

With cold, dilute aqueous $\text{NaOH}$, chlorine forms chloride and chlorate(I). With hot, concentrated aqueous $\text{NaOH}$, it forms chloride and chlorate(V).

Cold reaction:
$$\text{Cl}_2 + 2\text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{NaCl} + \text{NaClO} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

Hot reaction:
$$3\text{Cl}_2 + 6\text{NaOH} \rightarrow 5\text{NaCl} + \text{NaClO}_3 + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Identify the other ion**

The question tells you one product is $\text{Cl}^-$, where Cl is -1. The question states the NaOH is hot, so the second chlorine-containing ion must be the more oxidised one from the hot equation.

That ion is chlorate(V), $\text{ClO}_3^-$, where Cl has oxidation state +5.

options.A: Incorrect. $\text{ClO}^-$ is chlorate(I), hypochlorite. This is formed with cold, dilute NaOH, not hot NaOH. It is the classic trap of mixing up the two temperature conditions.
options.B: Incorrect. $\text{ClO}_2^-$ is chlorite, with Cl in the +3 state. This ion is not formed in the disproportionation of chlorine with NaOH under either cold or hot conditions.
options.C: Correct. Hot aqueous NaOH gives disproportionation to $\text{Cl}^-$ and $\text{ClO}_3^-$. This matches the balanced equation $3\text{Cl}_2 + 6\text{NaOH} \rightarrow 5\text{NaCl} + \text{NaClO}_3 + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}$, where chlorine is reduced to -1 and oxidised to +5.
options.D: Incorrect. $\text{ClO}_4^-$ is perchlorate, with Cl in the +7 state. This requires much stronger oxidising conditions and is not produced by simply heating chlorine with NaOH.
